recording.trigger: m (sustained motion, indoors, still on home Wi-Fi)
recording.note: raw file stays in the ignored data/raw tree; the site holds the same session

protocol: board held in front of the chest with both hands, no arm swing, indoors: trigger walk, 2 min still, ~1.5 min normal walk, ~1 min fast walk (in that order), then still until the 5 min rule ended the session

thresholds.not_calibrated: run: nobody has run with the board; 600 mg is a guess above the ~610 mg transient seen when it was set down
thresholds.applies_to: this device and this mounting; a dog wearing it on a harness needs its own calibration

findings: rest and walk separate by a factor of about 25 (rest p90 4.2 mg, walk p10 102.9 mg), so the boundary is not sensitive: 149 of 149 labelled windows agreed

the dominant frequency reflects how the board is carried, not the gait: the fast phase read 1.88 Hz by FFT and 2.00 Hz by autocorrelation, which is a 120 steps/min cadence, while the slower normal-walk phase read 3.38/2.86 Hz - too fast to be a cadence. Held in front of the chest the arms act as a spring and their 2-5 Hz sway dominates while the torso bounce is small; it only takes over once the walk is brisk enough. Both estimators agree, so this is the mounting, not the algorithm. Classification therefore uses amplitude, whose ordering was correct (fast walk > normal walk > rest)
a single 610 mg window when the board was set down was classified as run; lone first/last windows now follow their neighbour
a harness-mounted box is rigidly coupled to the trunk, so the fundamental should be the dog's step frequency; check this on the first worn recording before trusting frequency for the walk/run split
